meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: I must not get nervous right now at all.
And right now excuse me.
Listen, tell me right now.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'district prefect' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Today the prefect will be at the grand opening.
Right now the prefect will cut our ribbon.

meanings.note: Prefix 'пере-' denotes crossing over, repeating, or exceeding a limit (stem 'резать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'will cut'.

examples.text: Надо всё сделать и перерезать вовремя.
examples.trans: We need to do everything and will cut on time.

examples.text: На нашей кухне все умеют перерезать.
examples.trans: In our kitchen everyone knows how to will cut.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'our', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: В нашем отеле действует новая услуга.
examples.trans: A new service operates in our hotel.
This is a service for our guests.
Do not disturb our rest.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'ribbon' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Are you satisfied now?

examples.text: Ты моя жизнь и моя вселенная.
examples.trans: You are my life and my universe.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'applause' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Applause, ladies and gentlemen!

examples.text: Красивая дама сидела у большого окна.

examples.text: Та симпатичная дама из соседнего ресторана.
examples.trans: That pretty lady from the neighboring restaurant.

meanings.en: to come, arrive (idiomatic in добро пожаловать = welcome)
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'жаловать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to come, grant', paired with 'жаловать'.

examples.trans: Welcome to our hotel!
Welcome to the hotel!

examples.text: Добро пожаловать в наш новый дом!
examples.trans: Welcome to our new home!

examples.trans: Strong contractions.

meanings.note: Agent/instrument noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-тель' ('-er'). Common masculine noun meaning 'hotel' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: В нашем отеле действует новая услуга.
examples.trans: A new service operates in our hotel.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Strong contractions.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'my', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh my God.

examples.text: Ну что, Витя, теперь ты мой раб.
examples.trans: Well then, Vitya, now you are my servant.

examples.text: Я хочу, чтобы ты приготовил пиццу.

examples.trans: Come on, everything is fine.
Come on, that is all.

examples.text: Я знаю всё в моём отеле.
examples.trans: I know everything in my hotel.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'will be'.

examples.trans: And what should I do?
And I do not want to be anyone else.
I have a toy car.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I must not get nervous right now at all.
I have no idea.
No, nothing.

meanings.note: Privative prefix 'бес-' ('without, -less', before voiceless consonants) (stem 'покоиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'worry', paired with 'забеспокоиться'.

examples.trans: Don't worry.
Mum is worried.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'came, arrived (she)', paired with 'приезжать'.

examples.trans: The hot pizza arrived, delivery.
Which car did you come in?
Pasha has arrived.

meanings.en: hot (to the touch, of food/drink, not weather)
meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('hot').

examples.trans: The hot pizza arrived, delivery.
Arkasha, here's some hot tea.
Careful, the cup is very hot.

meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'ставка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'delivery' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The hot pizza arrived, delivery.
There's pizza delivery here.
Delivery runs twenty-four hours a day.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'who', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Никто не будет командовать на моей кухне!
examples.trans: Nobody is going to give orders in my kitchen!
Victoria Sergeevna, people came to see you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We work better than everyone here.

examples.text: Сейчас мы быстро наведём здесь порядок!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'let's', paired with 'дать'.

examples.trans: Come on, everything is fine.
